 Joseph Gordon-Levitt warns of generative AI’s real risk: who controls it
 He says a few firms dominate training, deployment, and oversight
 Manuel Bosque 
 October 19, 2026
 Updated: October 19, 2026 at 10:16 AM
 Joseph Gordon-Levitt says the real danger in generative AI isn’t some sci-fi wave of killer robots. It’s the small group of companies building the technology, training it, and deciding how it gets used. Speaking as the United Nations’ first Global Advocate for Human-centric Digital Governance, he says the argument should stay centered on transparency, accountability, and public oversight, especially now that private firms are reshaping search, workplace software, entertainment, education, and communication. Put that much power in that few hands, he argues, and you’re getting uncomfortably close to totalitarianism.
 Gordon-Levitt is also pushing for “residuals for data,” which would give creators a share of the profits when their writing, images, and performances are used to train commercial models.
 ChatGPT 
 Download 
 And the stakes aren’t small. Creative generative tools are projected to reach $14.03 billion by 2030 , while the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) says artists’ income could fall by 2028, with routine creative work likely to get hit first. Critics also warn that non-Western perspectives, other sectors supplying training data, and smaller companies are being squeezed out by the sheer cost of building large models.
 If you’re paying attention to how AI could change the way you work, search, communicate, and create, this is a warning worth taking seriously .
 You can already see the fight taking shape in the United States, which still doesn’t have a full federal AI law, in the European Union’s risk-based rules, which still leave creator pay and data use unresolved, and in chatbot designs meant to keep you engaged through nudges that steer behavior.
